title: The Word was made flesh (John 1:9–14)
hookLine: and dwelt among us; Catholics once genuflected at this line in nearly every Mass

lines: THE PRIEST READS JOHN IN LATIN.
cards: Et Verbum caro factum est. In the old Latin Mass, the Mass is over, or nearly.
The priest has given the blessing, and now he walks to the left side of the altar and reads in Latin from the first chapter of John, a reading called the Last Gospel. The people are standing.
They know where this is going. They are waiting for one line. When it comes, priest and people go down on one knee together.

teach.b: Before the line, John tells a hard truth. The true light came into the world, and the world, made by him, didn't know him. "He came unto his own, and his own received him not."
But some did, and to them he gave power to become children of God.
Then the line: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." In Latin, Et Verbum caro factum est. That's where they knelt.

Yesterday the Word was with God before creation. Today the same Word has skin, and hunger, and a mother. Flesh is a blunt word: not a body, or a human nature, but the soft, mortal, breakable stuff we're made of.
The Greek verb literally means pitched his tent, and readers hear in it the tabernacle in the desert, the tent where God's glory came to dwell among Israel.
John goes on: "and we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." The Church calls this the Incarnation, from the Latin for in the flesh.
The genuflection at the Last Gospel is mostly gone now, since that reading left the ordinary form of the Mass after the Second Vatican Council. But the gesture lives on.

teach.h: STILL WE BOW AT THESE WORDS.
teach.b: In the Creed, at the words about the Son becoming man, Catholics bow; on Christmas and the feast of the Annunciation, they kneel at those words instead. Those who pray the Angelus traditionally kneel at this very line.
The body bends at the moment God is said to take a body.

how: Catholics bow at the words of the Incarnation in the Creed and genuflect there on Christmas and the Annunciation; those who pray the Angelus traditionally kneel at "and the Word was made flesh".

o: he pitched his tent among us
he spoke the world into being
he knelt down before the people

s: the Last Gospel is still read at every Mass
it left the ordinary form after the Second Vatican Council. it remains in the traditional Latin Mass.
Catholics bow at the Incarnation in the Creed
and on Christmas and the Annunciation, they kneel instead.
dwelt translates a word meaning pitched a tent
the Greek recalls the desert tabernacle, where God's glory dwelt.

games.q: you're John, writing the line at the heart of your opening. you want to say God's Word became human. which word do you choose?
o: he took on a human nature.
games.why: John chose flesh, the blunt word for soft, mortal stuff, and dwelt, literally pitched his tent among us.

practice: Stand or sit tall, and say the words slowly: and the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. At made flesh, bow your head, or bend at the waist, or kneel if that's your way, and hold it for a breath before coming back up.
If you pray, let the bow be your prayer; if you don't, just notice what it is to bend your body at a thought.

wordCard.voice: Eskenosen. John's word for dwelt, pitched his tent: the eternal Word who took on a human body and lived among us. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he pitched his tent, dwelt (John 1:14); from skēnē, a tent, the word used for the tabernacle.

carryVoice: Your line: and dwelt among us. The Word chose an address of his own. See you tomorrow.
